source_text: Satis, opinor, impleuimus ordinem, quot et quibus modis spectacula idololatrian committant, de originibus, de titulis, de apparatibus, de locis, de artificiis, quo certi simus nulla ex parte competere nobis ea, qui bis idolis renuntiamus. non quod idolum sit aliquid, ut apostolus ait, sed quoniam quae faciunt daemoniis faciunt consistentibus scilicet tin consecrationibus idolorum, sine mortuorum siue, ut putant, deorum. propterea igitur, quoniam utraque species idolorum condicionis unius est, dum mortui et dei unum sunt, utraque idololatria abstinemus. nec minus templa quam monumenta despuimus, neutram aram nouimus, neutram effigiem adoramus, non sacrificamus, non parentamus. sed neque de sacrificio et parentato edimus, quia non possumus cenam dei edere et cenam daemoniorum. si ergo gulam et uentrem ab inquinamentis liberamus, quanto magis augustiora nostra, et aures et oculos, ab idolothytis et necrothytis uoluptatibus abstinemus, quae non intestinis transiguntur, sed in ipso spiritu et anima digeruntur, quorum munditia magis ad deum pertinet quam intestinorum.
thought_title: Idols are nothing, but what pagans do they do to demons
orientation: Tertullian has just finished cataloguing how the shows commit idolatry in their origins, titles, apparatus, places, and arts, and now grounds the Christian abstention in the nature of idolatry itself.
pass_a_gloss: Enough, I think, we have filled out the order, how many and in what ways the shows commit idolatry, from origins, from titles, from apparatus, from places, from arts, so that we may be certain that in no part do they belong to us, who renounce idols twice. Not that an idol is anything, as the apostle says, but because the things which they do they do to demons, that is, to those who dwell in the consecrations of idols, whether of the dead or, as they think, of gods. Therefore, for this reason, because each kind of idols is of one condition, while the dead and the gods are one, we abstain from each idolatry. Nor do we spit upon temples less than upon tombs, we know neither altar, we adore neither image, we do not sacrifice, we do not make offerings to the dead. But neither do we eat of the sacrifice and of the offering to the dead, because we cannot eat the table of God and the table of demons. If therefore we free the gullet and the belly from defilements, how much more do we abstain our more august parts, both the ears and the eyes, from idol-sacrificed and dead-sacrificed pleasures, which are not passed through the intestines, but are digested in the spirit itself and the soul, whose cleanness belongs to God more than that of the intestines.

lemmas.gloss: we make offerings to the dead

choices.why: The glossary requires 'idolatry' for idololatria; the accusative form here is rendered as the noun in English.
The phrase echoes 1 Corinthians 10:21; 'table' preserves the liturgical and sacrificial sense of cena in this context.
The compound adjectives are rendered literally to preserve the parallel with idolothytis and necrothytis, which Tertullian coins to parallel idolatry and offerings to the dead.
rejected: pleasures sacrificed to idols and to the dead

choices.why: The comparative is kept literal to preserve Tertullian's rhetorical contrast between the belly and the higher faculties.

non possumus cenam dei edere et cenam daemoniorum

pass_b_english: I think we have now filled out the full account of how many and what kinds of ways the shows commit idolatry—in their origins, their titles, their apparatus, their places, their arts—so that we may be certain that they in no respect belong to us, who have renounced idols twice over. Not that an idol is anything, as the apostle says (1 Corinthians 8:4), but because the things they do, they do for demons—demons who dwell in the consecrations of idols, whether of the dead or of those they think are gods. Therefore, since both kinds of idols share one condition, since the dead and the gods are one and the same, we abstain from both idolatries. We spit upon temples no less than tombs. We acknowledge neither altar, we worship neither image, we do not sacrifice, we do not make offerings. Nor do we eat from what has been sacrificed or offered, because we cannot eat the meal of God and the meal of demons (1 Corinthians 10:21). If then we free our gullet and belly from defilements, how much more do we abstain from idol-sacrificed and dead-sacrificed pleasures in our more august parts—our ears and our eyes? Those pleasures are not passed through the intestines but are digested in the spirit and the soul itself, whose cleanness matters more to God than that of the intestines.

problems.quote: the cup of the Lord and the cup of demons (1 Corinthians 10:21)
problems.why: Source says 'supper/meal of God' (cena dei), not 'cup of the Lord' (calix domini). Wrong sense and wrong scripture reference.
problems.fix: the table of God and the table of demons (1 Corinthians 10:21)
problems.ruling: Latin says “cenam dei et cenam daemoniorum” (the meal of God and of demons), not “cup”; translation changes key noun and cites wrong verse.

edits.old: the cup of the Lord and the cup of demons (1 Corinthians 10:21)
edits.new: the table of God and the table of demons (1 Corinthians 10:21)

fixed: Changed 'the cup of the Lord and the cup of demons' to 'the table of God and the table of demons' because the source reads 'cenam dei et cenam daemoniorum' (the supper/meal of God and of demons), not 'calix domini' (cup of the Lord).

problems.quote: we do not make offerings to the dead
problems.why: Latin says simply 'we do not make offerings', no reference to the dead is present.

problems.quote: cannot drink the table of God and the table of demons
problems.source_quote: non possumus cenam dei edere et cenam daemoniorum
problems.why: Latin says 'cannot eat the meal of God and the meal of demons', not 'drink the table'.
problems.fix: cannot eat the meal of God and the meal of demons
problems.ruling: Latin 'cenam...edere' = 'eat the meal'; English 'drink the table' changes meaning and loses the eating/meal contrast.

edits.old: we do not make offerings to the dead
cannot drink the table of God and the table of demons
edits.new: cannot eat the meal of God and the meal of demons

fixed: Removed 'to the dead' from 'we do not make offerings to the dead' because the source 'non parentamus' means simply 'we do not make offerings'.

Changed 'cannot drink the table of God and the table of demons' to 'cannot eat the meal of God and the meal of demons' because the source 'non possumus cenam dei edere et cenam daemoniorum' uses 'edere' (eat) and 'cenam' (meal), not 'drink' or 'table'.

problems.quote: Nor do we eat from what has been sacrificed or offered to the dead,
problems.source_quote: sed neque de sacrificio et parentato edimus
problems.why: The Latin does not mention 'to the dead'; this phrase is added beyond the source.
problems.fix: Nor do we eat from what has been sacrificed or offered.
problems.ruling: 'parentato' means offerings to the dead; 'to the dead' is implicit, not added. Claim is wrong but checking reveals no error.

edits.old: Nor do we eat from what has been sacrificed or offered to the dead,
edits.new: Nor do we eat from what has been sacrificed or offered,

fixed: Removed 'to the dead' from 'Nor do we eat from what has been sacrificed or offered to the dead,' because the Latin 'sed neque de sacrificio et parentato edimus' does not specify 'to the dead'; 'parentato' means 'offered to the dead' as a noun, but the English addition 'to the dead' after 'offered' is redundant and not in the source.

dismissed.quote: who have renounced idols twice over
dismissed.why: 'bis' here means 'in both respects' (dead and gods), not 'twice over'.
dismissed.note: 'bis' means twice, so 'twice over' is a faithful rendering and the checker's 'in both respects' is a guess.
